title: The Centurion: Faith Outside the “Chosen”
paragraphs: The Centurion: Faith Outside the “Chosen”
You thought being close to religion meant being close to God.
You thought knowing the language, carrying the label, standing near the temple, sitting near the truth, made you safe.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
You can grow up around the things of God and still miss God Himself.
And someone you would never expect can recognize Jesus faster than the people who were raised with the promises.
That is the shock of the centurion.

A Roman soldier.
An outsider.
A man outside the covenant people.
A man not born among the “chosen.”
A man with no tribal inheritance in Israel.
And yet when he met Jesus, he saw what many in Israel refused to see:
Authority. Mercy. Lordship.
Read that again.
The scandal in the street
In Matthew 8:5–10, a centurion comes to Jesus pleading for his servant:

“Lord, my servant is lying at home paralyzed, dreadfully tormented.”
Jesus said to him, “I will come and heal him.”
The centurion answered and said, “Lord, I am not worthy that You should come under my roof. But only speak a word, and my servant will be healed…”
“When Jesus heard it, He marveled, and said to those who followed, ‘Assuredly, I say to you, I have not found such great faith, not even in Israel.’”
Not even in Israel.
Do you hear the weight of that?

The people with the Scriptures.
The people with the prophets.
The people with the covenants.
The people with the history.
And yet Jesus says this foreigner saw more clearly.
Why?
Because proximity to truth is not the same as surrender to truth.
Because heritage cannot replace repentance.
Because religion without faith is still unbelief.
The diagnosis nobody wants
You can be “chosen” in appearance and dead in heart.
You can know the stories and not know the Savior.
You can quote Scripture, defend doctrine, attend church, post verses, and still resist the authority of Jesus in the secret place.
God saw it.
You knew.

The centurion did not come with credentials.
He came with need.

He did not come demanding status.
He came confessing unworthiness.
“Lord, I am not worthy…”
That line alone exposes an entire generation trained to speak about God without trembling before Him.
The centurion understood two things many religious people still do not understand:

First, Jesus has absolute authority.
Second, he himself was absolutely undeserving.
That is where real faith begins.

Not with spiritual swagger.
With surrender.
Authority recognized by an outsider
The centurion says in essence: I know authority when I see it. I live under command, and I give commands. If You speak, sickness obeys.

He saw that Jesus did not merely pray for power.
Jesus carried power.

He did not see Jesus as a teacher only.
He saw Him as Lord.
This is the dividing line.

Many admire Jesus.
Few bow to Him.

Many want His compassion.
Few submit to His command.

Many want healing.
Few want holiness.
But the centurion saw both mercy and majesty in one Person.
That is faith.

Not vague spirituality.
Not emotional inspiration.
Not inherited tradition.
Faith is seeing Jesus rightly.
Law on one side. Grace on the other.
Israel had the Law. The covenants. The promises. The temple system.
“To them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises.” — Romans 9:4
Yet privilege became presumption for many.
They assumed closeness to sacred things guaranteed peace with God.
But Scripture crushes that lie.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
All.

Jew and Gentile.
Religious and irreligious.
Insider and outsider.

The problem was never merely ethnicity.
The problem was sin.

And the answer was never mere lineage.
The answer was Christ.
“Therefore know that only those who are of faith are sons of Abraham.” — Galatians 3:7
Read that again.
Only those who are of faith.

Not performance.
Not ancestry.
Not reputation.
Not your family’s Christianity.
Not your ministry résumé.
Not your church attendance streak.
Faith.
And even that faith is not faith in yourself, but faith in Jesus Christ.
Jesus breaks the walls men build
Then Jesus says something even more explosive:

“And I say to you that many will come from east and west, and sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. But the sons of the kingdom will be cast out into outer darkness.” — Matthew 8:11–12
This was not just a compliment to one soldier.
This was a warning shot to everyone trusting in spiritual entitlement.

Many from east and west.
Outsiders.
Far-off people.
Unexpected people.
People you wrote off.
People religion looked down on.
And some “sons of the kingdom” cast out.
Why?
Because being near the story is not the same as belonging to the King.
You can carry the badge and miss the banquet.
You can look like the insider and die as the stranger.
That should shake you.
The offense of grace
Religious pride hates this story.
Because grace does not move according to human ranking.
Grace humiliates the proud and welcomes the broken.

Grace does not ask, “Were you raised in the right atmosphere?”
Grace asks, “Do you believe the Son?”
“He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him. But as many as received Him, to them He gave the right to become children of God…” — John 1:11–12
As many as received Him.
That means the door swings open far wider than proud religion wanted.
But it also means the door is narrower than human self-righteousness can tolerate.
Because the door is not heritage.
The door is Jesus.
“I am the door. If anyone enters by Me, he will be saved…” — John 10:9

Not by bloodline.
Not by morality.
Not by nation.
Not by denomination.
By Me, Jesus says.
The centurion’s faith was not generic
This matters.
The centurion did not merely “believe in something.”
He believed Jesus could do what only God-authorized power could do.
His faith had an object.

Not positivity.
Not ritual.
Not sincerity by itself.
Jesus.
That is why salvation is not earned by being decent. It is received by grace through faith in Christ.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works…” — Ephesians 2:8–9
And this grace is necessary because sin is real.

Not mistakes.
Not flaws.
Not bad habits.
Sin.

Rebellion against a holy God.
Hidden filth.
Private compromise.
Open defiance.
Self-rule.
God saw it.
You knew.
And yet the same Christ who marveled at the centurion’s faith would go to the cross for sinners from every tribe and tongue.
“But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
That is the Gospel.

Not “try harder.”
Not “be more deserving.”
Not “earn your place among the chosen.”
The Gospel is this:

You are a sinner.
You cannot save yourself.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for sin and rose again.
Repent and believe the Gospel.
Receive mercy you did not earn.
Receive righteousness you could never produce.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior
And here is where this turns from history into confrontation.
Because some of you are not the centurion.
You are the crowd.

Close enough to watch.
Too proud to kneel.

Some of you have been around church so long that the shock is gone.
The cross is familiar.
The words are familiar.
The songs are familiar.
But your heart is still untouched.
Others of you feel disqualified, too far gone, too outside, too stained, too foreign to grace.
This story crushes both lies.

To the proud insider, Jesus says:
Your status cannot save you.

To the broken outsider, Jesus says:
Come. Believe Me.
That is why the centurion matters.
He is living proof that faith can appear where religion least expects it.
He is a warning that spiritual privilege can rot into unbelief.
He is a signpost pointing beyond ethnicity, beyond ceremony, beyond human categories, straight to Christ.
The real chosen question
People keep asking, “Who are the chosen?”
But here’s the deeper question:
Have you come to the Chosen One?
Because all the promises of God find their Yes in Christ.
“For all the promises of God in Him are Yes, and in Him Amen…” — 2 Corinthians 1:20

Outside of Christ, heritage cannot save you.
Inside Christ, grace can redeem you.
The centurion stood outside the covenant nation, but he came to the covenant Lord.
And that changed everything.
Decision moment
So where are you in this story?
Are you the religious insider trusting your nearness to holy things?

Or are you the humbled sinner who says,
“Lord, I am not worthy… but speak a word”?

One posture is condemned.
The other is commended.

One clings to identity without repentance.
The other falls at Jesus’ feet.

One assumes.
The other believes.
Repent.

Turn from sin.
Turn from pride.
Turn from empty religion.
Turn from self-trust.
And believe in Jesus Christ.

Not merely as helper.
As Lord.

Not merely as example.
As Savior.

Not merely as a name in your content.
As the King with authority to forgive, cleanse, heal, and save.
Open loop for the soul
The scandal of the centurion is still happening.
People raised “inside” are walking away cold.
People once called “outside” are falling at the feet of Jesus in broken, trembling faith.
So do not trust the label.
Do not trust the crowd.
Do not trust your history.
Trust Christ.
And if a Roman centurion could recognize the glory of Jesus from outside the camp, what excuse will you give standing this close to the truth?
Read that again.
